Using a weak password to protect a Java keystore with a public certificate is not sufficient to protect the truststore. The truststore, which contains private keys, is a separate entity from the keystore. The keystore is used to store public certificates, while the truststore is used to store private keys. 

If a weak password is used to protect the truststore, it would not provide any additional security benefits. In fact, it would make it easier for an attacker to access the private keys, as they would have access to the password. 

Additionally, using a weak password for the truststore would also make it vulnerable to password cracking attacks, as an attacker could potentially use a brute-force attack to guess the password.
candidate_qwen3_32b: The Java keystore stores both public certificates (for trust) and private keys (for authentication and encryption). A weak password protecting the keystore allows attackers to decrypt and access private keys, enabling them to impersonate services, decrypt sensitive data, or sign malicious content. Even if the truststore (for trusted certificates) is public, the keystore's private keys must remain confidential. A weak password undermines this confidentiality, exposing the system to man-in-the-middle attacks, data breaches, and unauthorized access. Therefore, using a strong password is essential to secure the keystore.

question:
Does the ECDSA signature value (of an OCSP response) need to be DER encoded

In OCSP responses by a certain eIDAS PKI I every once in a while get signature values which, when unpacked from their BIT STRING, contain an ECDSA signature whose INTEGER constituents have an unnecessary leading 00 byte and, therefore, are not DER encoded, e.g.
 376   10: . . . . . SEQUENCE {
 378    8: . . . . . . OBJECT IDENTIFIER ecdsaWithSHA256 (1 2 840 10045 4 3 2)
         : . . . . . . . (ANSI X9.62 ECDSA algorithm with SHA256)
         : . . . . . . }
 388   71: . . . . . BIT STRING, encapsulates {
 391   68: . . . . . . SEQUENCE {
 393   32: . . . . . . . INTEGER    
         : . . . . . . . . 6D 7F 95 D5 8E 9B E1 18    m.......
         : . . . . . . . . 60 DC A6 D6 91 37 0D B4    `....7..
         : . . . . . . . . AF D5 C9 A0 E8 21 40 4A    .....!@J
         : . . . . . . . . 94 8B 9F AA 6C DC F2 8C                            
 427   32: . . . . . . . INTEGER    
         : . . . . . . . . 00 1B FD 92 CB 1E E2 A8    ........
         : . . . . . . . . 2B 18 FC 37 ED 42 D0 66    +..7.B.f
         : . . . . . . . . E6 52 63 88 47 88 EE 00    .Rc.G...
         : . . . . . . . . FF 37 CF 20 8F F8 3C C1                            
         : . . . . . . . . Error: Integer has non-DER encoding.
         : . . . . . . . }
         : . . . . . . }

Here already the ASN.1 dump utility claims that this non-DER encoding is an error, and so does the current BouncyCastle version (a check for DER encoding has been introduced in a October 2016 commit, unfortunately without any issue or norm reference in the comment).
I would like to know whether BouncyCastle is too strict or the OCSP responder indeed creates invalid responses. Unfortunately I have not yet found any norm (relevant for eIDAS PKIs) which clearly indicates which encoding may be used there.
RFC 6960 on OCSP says

The value for response SHALL be the DER encoding of
  BasicOCSPResponse.
BasicOCSPResponse       ::= SEQUENCE {
   tbsResponseData      ResponseData,
   signatureAlgorithm   AlgorithmIdentifier,
   signature            BIT STRING,
   certs            [0] EXPLICIT SEQUENCE OF Certificate OPTIONAL }

but this only requires the BIT STRING signature to be DER encoded, not any data encapsulated in it.
TR-03111 (Technical Guideline on Elliptic Curve Cryptography by the German Federal Office for Information Security) says

In X9.62 format the ECDSA-signature (r; s) is encoded as ASN.1 structure with the following
  syntax:
ECDSA-Sig-Value ::= SEQUENCE {
  r INTEGER,
  s INTEGER
}

To embed the signature in a BIT STRING the DER encoded ECDSA-Sig-Value SHALL be the
  value of the bit string (including tag and length eld).

but a requirement by the German Federal Office for Information Security hardly is normative for eIDAS PKIs in general.
In X9.62 I only find

While it is likely that these
  ASN.1 definitions will be encoded using the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER), other encoding rules may also
  be used.
candidate_llama_3_2_1b_instruct: No. The ECDSA signature value in an OCSP response is not necessarily DER encoded. According to the RFC 6960, the response SHALL be the DER encoding of the BasicOCSPResponse, which includes the BIT STRING containing the signature.
candidate_qwen3_32b: Yes, the ECDSA signature value in an OCSP response must be DER encoded. According to RFC 6960, the `signature` field is a BIT STRING that contains the DER encoding of the signature value. While the standard does not explicitly re-encode the BIT STRING contents, DER is the required encoding for ASN.1 structures in cryptographic contexts, including ECDSA signatures. TR-03111 explicitly mandates DER encoding for ECDSA-Sig-Value when embedded in a BIT STRING. X9.62 allows other encodings but DER is the de facto standard for interoperability. The presence of a leading 00 byte in the INTEGER indicates non-DER encoding, which is invalid. BouncyCastle is correct to reject it.

question:
How does WifiKill work?

How is possible for Wifi Kill to block someone from using Wi-Fi, even if you don't have access to the router settings and you even don't use MITM (I think)?
answer:
By using disassocate packets. 
Those packets has the source MAC of an AP and force the client to disconnect and reconnect to the AP.  
By keeping sending those packets, you can keep any client away and unable to connect to this specific access point. 
Edit:  A summery for people can't access links.
From a tool named Aircrack-ng
Deauthentication
Description
This attack sends disassocate packets to one or more clients which are currently associated with a particular access point. Disassociating clients can be done for a number of reasons:

Recovering a hidden ESSID. This is an ESSID which is not being broadcast. Another term for this is “cloaked”.
Capturing WPA/WPA2 handshakes by forcing clients to reauthenticate.
Generate ARP requests (Windows clients sometimes flush their ARP cache when disconnected)

Of course, this attack is totally useless if there are no associated wireless client or on fake authentications.

Note: Some clients ignore broadcast deauthentications. If this is the case, you will need to send a deauthentication directed at the particular client.

Source: http://www.aircrack-ng.org/doku.php?id=deauthentication
candidate_llama_3_2_1b_instruct:
Wi-Fi Kill is a type of attack that exploits the fact that Wi-Fi networks often use a technique called "EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol)" to authenticate users. EAP is a protocol that allows devices to authenticate with a network using a username and password.
